newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa privatisation earmarks shares for staff.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa privatisation earmarks shares for staff.

text.p: Employees of privatised South African state enterprises will be granted options to purchase up to 10,000 rand worth of shares in their companies, Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said on Monday.

State firms set for full or partial privatisation are also being required to set aside equity for the National Empowerment Fund, designed to help historically disadvantaged sections of the community, she told a pan-African privatisation conference.
Sigcau said 1997 would be the year in which South Africa's privatisation programme reaped tangible benefits.
The government plans to complete the sale of a 30 percent stake in telecoms giant Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium, raising "several billion rand" for the state, she said.

Analaysts estimate the sale of the stake -- the first big deal in the country's privatisation programme -- could net around six billion rand. Much of this is expected to be used to improve telecommunications infrastructure, but Sigcau said cutting government debt was also a goal of asset sales.

"Privatisation proceeds will enable government to retire debt, to reduce interest payments and to free capital for social needs such as housing, education, healthcare, crime prevention and the provision of basic services."

A further 10 percent of Telkom equity will be provided for black empowerment, a pattern Sigcau said would be duplicated in other upcoming privatisations this year in the tourism, transport, mining and forestry sectors.
"Each of these state-owned enterprises will be required to implement an employee share ownership scheme and make available equity to the National Emowerment Fund (NEF)," she said.
The government had approved in principle the granting of options to all employees for the purchase of up to 10,000 rand worth of shares, she said.
These shares would be offered at a discount, as would shares offered to the NEF.
The aim was to promote wide ownership of the country's productive assets, to stimulate savings among a wider section of the population and to motivate staff.

Sigcau said it had taken time to gain consensus on privatisation as a central part of the restructuring of state assets inherited from the apartheid era and she rejected charges that the government had been dragging its feet.
But the decisions had now been taken and South Africa was about to see the biggest privatisation programme on the African continent.

"I can now say the 'P' word with confidence...The South African government has embarked on plans to launch what I believe is by far the largest and most wide-ranging restructuring of state assets seen to date."
